chapter.title: Arrays, Collections and References
chapter.para: A .NET array is a Rexx Array, from 1, as BSF4ooRexx makes Java's arrays; every other collection keeps the indexing .NET documents for it (from 0 for a list, by key for a dictionary). Both work with DO OVER and DO WITH.

section.title: .NET Arrays
section.para: A .NET array comes to Rexx as a , which behaves as a Rexx Array: from 1 in every dimension, with a[i], a[i, j] = v, at, put, items, size, dimension, dimensions, hasIndex, makeArray, supplier, and makeString and toString as an Array's, so that say a shows its elements. It is still the .NET array, by reference: .NET sees what Rexx puts, its own members work (a~Length, a~Rank, 0-based as .NET's), and it goes back to .NET as itself.

Where it differs from a Rexx Array, it is because a .NET array has a fixed size and a type: items counts every element, not only those that hold a value; null elements are &nil; in DO OVER; one past the end is an error that says the length rather than &nil; or a bigger array; and an element that is put is converted to the array's element type (putStrict forces another type). A wrong index raises what a Rexx Array raises: 93.907 for a[0], 93.925 and 93.926 for too few or too many indexes. A jagged array (int[][]) is an array of arrays: jag[2] is a NetArray, jag[2][3] its element. An array whose lower bounds are not 0 (COM's arrays start at 1: Excel's Range.Value) is from 1 here as well; its own GetValue takes .NET's positions.

example.title: .NET arrays as Rexx Arrays
example.programlisting:
bytes = .net~System~Text~Encoding~UTF8~GetBytes("abc") say bytes[1] bytes~items bytes~dimension bytes~Length bytes[1] = 65 say .net~System~Text~Encoding~UTF8~GetString(bytes) bytes~makeString("L", ",") grid = .net~System~Array~CreateInstance(.net~type("int"), 2, 3) grid[2, 3] = 7 do with index i item v over grid if v \= 0 then say i~makeString("L", ",") "=" v end say grid~dimensions~makeString("L", ",") grid~hasIndex(2, 3) grid~hasIndex(3, 1) com = .net~System~Array~CreateInstance(.net~type("string"), .array~of(2), .array~of(1)) com[1] = "first" say com~GetLowerBound(0) com[1] com~GetValue(1) signal on syntax name past say bytes[4] past: say condition("O")~message signal on syntax say bytes[0] syntax: say condition("O")~code
::requires "net.cls"

section.title: Rexx Arrays to .NET
section.para: A one-dimensional Rexx Array goes to a .NET array, a List<T> or an IEnumerable<T> parameter as a new one, its items converted to T (a copy). A multidimensional Array goes to a .NET array of the same rank (int[,] for such a parameter, else object[,]), the item a[i, j] at [i - 1, j - 1]; it goes to nothing else, as a list would lose its shape. An omitted item is null where .NET takes one (an object[] or a string[]: the size is kept; an int[] cannot take it). The copy keeps the structure of the Arrays: one that contains itself is an object[] that contains itself, Arrays that contain each other keep the cycle, and one Array that appears twice is one .NET array (each argument is copied on its own; Arrays nested more than 1000 deep are an error). To a RexxObject (or object) parameter the Array goes as itself, by reference: an overload that takes it so wins over a copy.

example.title: Rexx Arrays given to .NET
example.programlisting:
say .net~System~String~Join("-", .array~of("a", "b", "c")) grid = .array~new(2, 3) do i = 1 to 2; do j = 1 to 3; grid[i, j] = i * 10 + j; end; end list = .net~System~Collections~ArrayList~new list~Add(grid) g = list~Item(0) -- the .NET array, as a Rexx Array again say .net~typeOf(g) g~Rank g~GetLength(1) g[2, 3]
::requires "net.cls"

example.title: Sparse Arrays, and Arrays in Arrays
example.programlisting:
s = .array~new(4); s[1] = "a"; s[3] = "c" say .net~System~String~Join("+", s) -- the size kept: nulls a = .array~of(1, 2); a~append(a) -- an Array that contains itself list = .net~System~Collections~ArrayList~new list~Add(a) copy = list~Item(0) say copy~length (copy[3] == copy)
::requires "net.cls"

section.title: Lists, Dictionaries and Indexers
section.para: Every collection that is not an array keeps .NET's own indexing: o[i] and o[i] = v are the type's indexer (its default member: Item, or what the type calls it, as StringBuilder's Chars), from 0 for a list, by key for a dictionary, with overloads chosen as for methods. An indexed property with another name is a message with arguments: o~Item(i).

A collection with both an integer indexer and a string one (NameValueCollection, Windows Forms' ListView.Items and Controls) takes a Rexx whole number as a position, as a COM collection does; a key that looks like a number is given with .net~string(k). This is the one place where a Rexx string does not prefer a string parameter ().

A StringTable or a Directory goes to a parameter that is a dictionary with string keys as a new Dictionary<string, T> with its entries, each value converted to T (a copy). An instance of a subclass of either class goes the same way. The keys are as stored: d~name = v stores NAME, d["name"] = v keeps the case.

example.title: Lists, dictionaries and indexers
example.programlisting:
d = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<string, int>")~new d["one"] = 1; d["two"] = 2 say d["two"] d~Count d~ContainsKey("one") l = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<string>")~new l~Add("a"); l~Add("b") say l[0] l[1] nv = .net~System~Collections~Specialized~NameValueCollection~new nv~Add("1", "first"); nv~Add("0", "second") say nv[0] "/" nv[.net~string(0)] "/" nv["1"] st = .stringTable~new; st["x"] = 1; st["y"] = 2 copy = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<string, int>")~new(st) say copy~Count copy["y"]
::requires "net.cls"

section.title: DO OVER and DO WITH
section.para: DO x OVER o gives the items of any IEnumerable (makeArray): a dictionary's items are its KeyValuePairs, as C#'s foreach gives them. DO WITH INDEX i ITEM v OVER o (supplier) gives indexes that o[i] takes back: a dictionary's keys and values, a list's positions from 0, an array's from 1 (an Array of positions for a multidimensional one), and 1 to n for any other enumerable. Both take a snapshot when the loop starts, so the loop may change the collection. An enum type is enumerable too: its values with DO OVER, its numbers and names with DO WITH ().

example.title: DO OVER and DO WITH
example.programlisting:
d = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<string, int>")~new d["one"] = 1; d["two"] = 2 do with index k item v over d; say k v; end do pair over d; say pair~Key"="pair~Value; end l = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<string>")~new l~Add("a"); l~Add("b") do with index i item x over l; say i x; end
::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: one 1 two 2 one=1 two=2 0 a 1 b

section.title: ref, out and in Parameters
section.para: A parameter passed by reference takes a , made by .net~ref([value]): after the call, its value is what the method left there. The call keeps its own result, as C#'s out var reads. An out parameter ignores the value given; a ref parameter converts it (&nil; for a value type is its default); an in parameter also takes a plain value, as in C#. A ref parameter does not take a plain value, and a NetRef fits no other kind of parameter.

example.title: ref and out parameters
example.programlisting:
d = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<string, int>")~new d["k"] = 42 r = .net~ref say d~TryGetValue("k", r) r~value n = .net~ref say .net~System~Int32~TryParse("x", n) n~value say .net~System~Int32~TryParse("123", n) n~value
::requires "net.cls"
